title: Understanding Religion in the Contemporary World
additionalRequisites: Students are welcome to take this course as a standalone half-unit. However, they may benefit from having previously taken AN290 (Anthropology and Religion). Any students with questions about their preparedness for the course are welcome to contact the course convenors.
availability: This course is available on the BA in Anthropology and Law, BA in Social Anthropology, BSc in Social Anthropology, Erasmus Reciprocal Programme of Study, Exchange Programme for Students from University of California, Berkeley, Exchange Programme for Students in Anthropology (Cape Town), Exchange Programme for Students in Anthropology (Fudan), Exchange Programme for Students in Anthropology (Melbourne) and Exchange Programme for Students in Anthropology (Tokyo). This course is freely available as an outside option to students on other programmes where regulations permit. It does not require permission. This course is freely available to General Course students. It does not require permission.
description: This course explores how religion manifests in a range of different societies, studying its relationship to broad social change including the rise of modernity and capitalism, the resurgence of nationalism and populism, as well as its codification in institutions such as the family, law, gender, and the state. We will critically evaluate the category of ‘religion’ and related concepts, paying attention to how these have been redefined in contemporary societies, and how such definitions affect ‘religious practice’ across the world. Throughout the course, emphasis is placed on the ethnographic record, including by foregrounding research that has been carried out by members of the anthropology department. The subject matter will be explored through carefully tailored research topics, each of which relates directly to the research interests of respective lecturers. Topics will relate to several ‘world religions’ and to forms of spirituality, as well as to secularism. Specific areas of focus may include: religious nationalism, religious freedom, the interface between sexuality and religion, transpersonal psychologies, sacrifice, religious conversion, doubt and conviction, martyrdom, New Age spirituality, and anthropological perspectives on ‘the secular’.
teaching: 15 hours of lectures and 10 hours of classes in the Winter Term.
formativeAssessment: Essay (1500 words). Students will have the opportunity to submit one formative essay of up to 1500 words during the course. Students will be informed of their formative submission deadline by email by the end of Week 3 of term.
